note: Subjects/Maths/FP1 Further Pure Mathematics 1/5 Matrix algebra integration.md
outline: Add and subtract matrices of equal order entrywise, and multiply every entry when scaling by a scalar. For products, match the inner dimensions and form each entry by a row-column dot product; in general $AB\ne BA$. A $2\times2$ determinant is $ad-bc$: zero means singular. A non-singular matrix has inverse $\frac1{ad-bc}\begin{pmatrix}d&-b\\-c&a\end{pmatrix}$. For invertible products, $(AB)^{-1}=B^{-1}A^{-1}$.

misconceptions.statement: Matrix subtraction or addition can be performed on mismatched positions or dimensions.
misconceptions.refutation: Only equal-sized matrices combine, entry by matching entry.
misconceptions.contrast: Check both dimensions; for subtraction keep the stated order.

misconceptions.statement: A scalar multiplies only one selected entry or one term in a matrix sum.
misconceptions.refutation: The scalar multiplies every entry, and distributes to both matrices in a sum.
misconceptions.contrast: Scale each whole matrix before combining entries.

misconceptions.statement: Matrix multiplication is entrywise or changing factor order has no effect.
misconceptions.refutation: Each product entry is a row-column dot product; generally $AB\ne BA$.
misconceptions.contrast: Check inner dimensions and preserve factor order.

misconceptions.statement: A $2\times2$ determinant is $ad+bc$, or any zero entry makes the matrix singular.
misconceptions.refutation: The determinant is $ad-bc$; singular means precisely $ad-bc=0$.
misconceptions.contrast: Calculate both diagonal products and subtract.

misconceptions.statement: The inverse of $AB$ is $A^{-1}B^{-1}$, or the adjugate needs no determinant divisor.
misconceptions.refutation: The product inverse reverses order, and $A^{-1}=\operatorname{adj}(A)/\det A$ for nonzero determinant.
misconceptions.contrast: Divide by the determinant and reverse factors in a product inverse.

FP1-5.1.motivate: When two tables of numbers describe the same positions, combining them entry by entry is natural. Matrix addition and subtraction formalise this, but the table sizes must agree.
FP1-5.1.establish: A matrix has an order: number of rows by number of columns. Two matrices are conformable for addition or subtraction only when both orders match. For equal-order matrices $A$ and $B$, the entry in row $i$, column $j$ of $A+B$ is $a_{ij}+b_{ij}$; in $A-B$ it is $a_{ij}-b_{ij}$. The result has the same order. Keep the order of subtraction: generally $A-B\ne B-A$.
FP1-5.1.connect: You can combine this entrywise rule with scalar multiplication to evaluate expressions such as $2A-3B$. Products of matrices follow a different rule.
FP1-5.1.note:
- Add and subtract only matrices of the same order.
- Combine entries in corresponding positions.
- In $A-B$, subtract each entry of $B$ from the matching entry of $A$.
FP1-5.1.self_explain: Why is a $2\times3$ matrix not conformable for addition with a $3\times2$ matrix, even though both have six entries?

discover.explanation: Both row and column counts must match.

FP1-5.2.motivate: Multiplying every measurement in a table by the same conversion factor should change every position, not just one. A scalar works the same way on a matrix.
FP1-5.2.establish: A scalar is an ordinary number. Scalar multiplication of a matrix means multiplying every entry by that number. If $A=\begin{pmatrix}a&b\\c&d\end{pmatrix}$, then $kA=\begin{pmatrix}ka&kb\\kc&kd\end{pmatrix}$. The order of the matrix stays the same. For matrices of the same order, $k(A+B)=kA+kB$, so a scalar distributes to both matrices. To calculate $pA-qB$, scale each matrix and then subtract matching entries.
FP1-5.2.connect: Scalar multiplication uses each entry independently; matrix multiplication uses rows and columns. Keeping those two procedures separate prevents a common error.
FP1-5.2.note:
- Multiply every matrix entry by the scalar.
- A negative scalar changes signs where appropriate.
- Distribute a scalar to both terms in a matrix sum.
FP1-5.2.self_explain: For $2A-3B$, why must the $3$ multiply every entry of $B$ before subtraction?

discover.explanation: The scalar multiplies every entry in each matrix.

FP1-5.3.motivate: A matrix product combines one row of information with one column at a time. The matching middle dimension tells you whether the pairing can be completed.
FP1-5.3.establish: For $AB$, the number of columns of $A$ must equal the number of rows of $B$: the matrices are then conformable for multiplication. If $A$ is $m\times n$ and $B$ is $n\times p$, then $AB$ is $m\times p$. Entry $(i,j)$ is the dot product of row $i$ of $A$ and column $j$ of $B$: multiply paired entries and add. This is not entrywise multiplication. In general $AB\ne BA$; a reverse product may even be undefined. Compatible products are associative, so $(AB)C=A(BC)$.
FP1-5.3.connect: Matrix multiplication defines the identity relation $AA^{-1}=I$. The order of factors also becomes crucial when inverting a product.
FP1-5.3.note:
- Check matching inner dimensions before multiplying.
- The outer dimensions give the product order.
- Each product entry is a row-column dot product.
- Preserve factor order; generally $AB\ne BA$.
FP1-5.3.self_explain: Why does a $2\times3$ matrix times a $3\times4$ matrix have order $2\times4$?

discover.explanation: The inner dimensions match, and the outer dimensions remain.

FP1-5.4.motivate: A determinant is a quick test for whether a square matrix can be undone by an inverse. For a $2\times2$ matrix, it takes one subtraction.
FP1-5.4.establish: For $A=\begin{pmatrix}a&b\\c&d\end{pmatrix}$, evaluate the $2\times2$ determinant as $\det A=ad-bc$: the main-diagonal product minus the other-diagonal product. A matrix is singular exactly when its determinant is zero; then it has no inverse. It is non-singular when its determinant is nonzero; then an inverse exists. A zero entry by itself does not make a matrix singular. For example, $\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\1&0\end{pmatrix}$ has determinant $-1$ and is non-singular.
FP1-5.4.connect: Compute the determinant before using the $2\times2$ inverse formula, since the determinant appears in its denominator.
FP1-5.4.note:
- For $\begin{pmatrix}a&b\\c&d\end{pmatrix}$, $\det A=ad-bc$.
- Zero determinant means singular and no inverse.
- Nonzero determinant means non-singular and invertible.
FP1-5.4.self_explain: Why can a matrix with one zero entry still be non-singular?

discover.explanation: Singularity depends on the determinant being zero, not on any single entry.

FP1-5.5.motivate: An inverse undoes a matrix operation. Its formula uses the determinant, and undoing two successive operations requires reversing their order.
FP1-5.5.establish: For a non-singular $2\times2$ matrix $A=\begin{pmatrix}a&b\\c&d\end{pmatrix}$, $A^{-1}=\frac{1}{ad-bc}\begin{pmatrix}d&-b\\-c&a\end{pmatrix}$. First check $ad-bc\ne0$; otherwise the inverse does not exist. Swap the diagonal entries, negate the off-diagonal entries and divide the whole matrix by the determinant. Verify an inverse using $AA^{-1}=A^{-1}A=I$. If $A$ and $B$ are invertible, $(AB)^{-1}=B^{-1}A^{-1}$. The order reverses because $(AB)(B^{-1}A^{-1})=A(BB^{-1})A^{-1}=I$.
FP1-5.5.connect: The determinant test comes first, and the matrix product rule lets you check the result. The identity matrix plays the role of $1$ in multiplication.
FP1-5.5.note:
- Invert only when $\det A\ne0$.
- Swap diagonal entries, negate off-diagonal entries, then divide by $\det A$.
- $AA^{-1}=I$ checks the inverse.
- $(AB)^{-1}=B^{-1}A^{-1}$ reverses order.
FP1-5.5.self_explain: Why does the inverse of $AB$ place $B^{-1}$ before $A^{-1}$?

discover.stem: Which expression equals $(AB)^{-1}$ for invertible matrices?
discover.explanation: Reversing the order makes adjacent factors cancel when you check the product against $I$.
